EICMA 2026 • MTPeak Stole Some of the Spotlight at EICMA 2026 With Insane Power and Retro Looks on Three Wheels
1967 Chevelle 4-Speed Is a True 138 SS 396 Time Capsule: 8,767 Miles, Knee Knocker, No One Wants It
73 photos
Photo: Mecum (2023)
When Chevrolet introduced the Chevelle for the 1964 model year, it created the most popular mid-size automobile ever built in Motor City. Across 3 generations spanning 1964 to 1977, General Motors produced approximately 4,880,000 Chevelles. To inject showroom excitement from day 1, Chevrolet launched the Super Sport trim in 1964 as the Malibu SS, selling 76,860 units equipped with inline-sixes or small-block 283-cubic-inch and 327-cubic-inch V8 engines up to 300 horsepower.
After adding the 350-horsepower 327-cubic-inch L79 V8 in 1965, Chevrolet unleashed the SS 396 mid-year under the Z16 option, building 201 cars with a 375-horsepower 396-cubic-inch V8. The SS 396 became a standalone series in 1966 with 72,272 units, followed by 63,006 in 1967 and 62,785 in 1968. Reclassified as an option package, it hit its all-time peak of 86,307 cars in 1969 before logging 53,599 units in 1970.
Before the Super Sport badge retired from the Chevelle lineup after 1973, buyers could also order 307-cubic-inch, 350-cubic-inch, and 454-cubic-inch V8 engines, capped by the 450-horsepower LS6 454 in 1970. Still, the first-generation 1967 SS 396 remains a collector favorite, which explains the buzz surrounding an Ermine White 1967 Chevelle SS 396 sport coupe recently advertised on Facebook without a listed price as a once-in-a-lifetime buy with 8,767 actual miles.
The brief social media listing touts a genuine 138-series Super Sport retaining its numbers-matching 396-cubic-inch V8, 4-speed manual transmission, factory AM/FM radio, knee-knocker tachometer, and original redline tires stored alongside the car. Bearing VIN 138177A179513, this hardtop rolled off the Atlanta, Georgia assembly line in June 1967 wearing code C-C Ermine White paint over a blue Strato-bucket seat interior.
Photo: Mecum (2023) Known on its show board as the Car From Coonbottom, the Chevelle was purchased new at Miller Chevrolet in Havana, Florida, by Willie Richardson. Living in the rural Coonbottom area outside Havana, Richardson took immense pride in his muscle car, sheltering it inside a wood-and-tin lean-to with tarps covering the open sides. For 20 years, he cranked the engine regularly, rarely drove the vehicle, and turned down every purchase offer.
When Richardson passed away in 1987, the odometer registered just 5,300 miles. His daughter inherited the coupe and promptly traded it toward a new car to David Stalling of Stalling's Motors in Cairo, Georgia. Fellow Cairo dealer Medford Stewart of Classic Auto Sales, who had chased the Chevelle for years, happened by Stalling's lot right after it arrived and immediately talked his friend into selling him the coveted low-mileage prize.
A February 1993 magazine feature also linked the 325-horsepower coupe to Quincy, Florida enthusiast Bo Deane before it spent several years in a local museum. William S. Brock of Quincy acquired the Chevelle in 1996, and its next owner bought it in November 1998 with 6,688 miles. Recently offered by Alexander Auto in Taylorsville, North Carolina, it also hit GAA Classic Cars in July 2026, stalling at a $77,000 high bid.
Photo: Mecum (2023) Having also appeared on Mecum in 2023 , eBay in December 2025, and duPont Registry before returning to GAA in November 2026, the coupe carries a December 5, 2022 certificate from Maryland appraiser Jerry MacNeish. MacNeish verified its original L35 325-horsepower 396-cubic-inch V8 engine paired with a Muncie M20 wide-ratio 4-speed transmission, and a Buffalo-cast rear axle exhibiting a factory stamping anomaly.
Despite its verified mileage and drivetrain, members of the Yenko.net Supercar Registry forum challenged early dealer descriptions calling the Chevelle an untouched time capsule. One commenter who inspected the Havana, Florida car nearly 20 years ago confirmed the mileage is authentic but lamented that the body received a full repaint instead of careful preservation. Forum experts also noted black-sprayed floors and frame rails, a re-spatter-painted trunk, and a repainted engine.
Both MacNeish and Yenko.net sleuths flagged the painted hood latch and hinges, which came in dark gray phosphate, alongside replacement hose clamps, cogged belts, and an added passenger-side mirror never available in 1967. Moreover, forum specialists observed that its U16 tachometer is a 1966 knee-knocker unit rather than a 1967 blinker tach, the U69 AM/FM radio conflicts with the leaning U73 rear antenna, and the wheels lack 6 A3 codes.
Photo: GAA Classic Cars Even with those cosmetic deviations, a low-mileage 1967 Chevelle SS 396 represents a cornerstone of Chevrolet performance. Among 403,963 Chevelles built for 1967, exactly 63,006 were domestic SS 396 models, split between 59,685 sport coupes starting at $2,825 and 3,321 convertibles priced at $3,033. Buyers could upgrade from the standard 325-horsepower L35 396 V8 to the 350-horsepower L34 for $105.35, or select the 375-horsepower solid-lifter L78 ordered on 612 cars.
On the street, the 1967 Chevelle SS 396 delivered serious muscle value, clocking a 0-to-60-mph sprint in 6.5 seconds and a 14.9-second quarter-mile run at 96.5 mph during period testing by Motor Trend. In the 1967 Detroit sales race, Chevrolet's 63,006 big-block intermediates trailed only the segment-leading Pontiac GTO, which found 81,722 buyers, while comfortably outpacing Oldsmobile's 24,829 Cutlass 4-4-2s, Ford's 20,700 Fairlane GTs, and Buick's 13,845 Skylark GS models.
Chrysler's big-block B-bodies posted smaller numbers in 1967, with Plymouth moving roughly 12,000 GTXs and Dodge building 10,809 Coronet R/Ts. This Chevy Chevelle SS 396 is hoping to break the curse that's been following it since 2023, and find a new owner, but the asking price is probably a personal matter between the seller and whoever is willing to haggle for it.
